_meta.title: Part-of-speech tags, and which words carry more than one
_meta.description:
Which categories a word can belong to. The load-bearing entries are the ones with MORE THAN ONE, because a single-category word can be read off morphology and a dual cannot. `plan` is noun and verb; so are `father`, `lesson`, `part`, `name`, `watch`, `phone` and `tire`. A parser holding a verb-only list treats every one of them as a predicate wherever it appears, which is how "My father has in his barn four hippoi" comes back with `father` as its verb.

This says what a word CAN be, never what it IS in a sentence. Choosing needs context — a determiner before it makes it a noun, a modal before it makes it a verb — and that rule belongs to the consumer, not to this file.
_meta.format: lemma -> a sorted string of category codes. `plan` is "nv"; `sharp` is "anrv".

stability.means: Use it freely — that is what CC BY is for — but do not assume it holds still. Content churns and the schema may change without notice. Pin a commit if you depend on the shape.

_meta.coverage: Webster's headword tags only. It is a 1913 dictionary, so it carries `hippo` but not `email`, and marks some senses archaic without saying so here. Absence means UNRECORDED.

_provenance._note: Recorded per batch, per the convention in base-verbs.json. `mined` = derived by code from a corpus named in PROVENANCE.md.

batches.commit_subject: pos-tags: what a word can be, from Webster's headwords

source.work: Webster's Unabridged Dictionary (1913) — public domain by age
source.finding: Every headword line of the form `Plan, n.` or `Phone, n. & v. t.`, with the syllable marks (" and *) stripped from the lemma. Webster's gives duals both ways — as separate entries for one spelling, and as a combined tag on one line — and both are collected. Fetched with --http1.1: over HTTP/2 the transfer dies at 20,905,986 of 28,956,350 bytes every time, which silently yields a dictionary ending mid-R.
